def: A network trained on human or AI comparisons to output a scalar score predicting which response is preferred. The target for RLHF and the selector for best-of-N.
A prompt with a preferred (chosen) and dispreferred (rejected) response, written \((x, y_w, y_l)\).
Models the probability that one item beats another as the logistic sigmoid of their score difference. The basis of reward model training and DPO.
How often independent labelers make the same choice on the same item. The practical ceiling on reward model accuracy.
A public benchmark (Lambert et al. 2024; RewardBench 2 in 2025) of preference pairs across chat, safety, and reasoning for comparing reward models.
Optimizing a proxy reward past the point where true quality peaks, so the proxy keeps rising while real quality falls. Quantified by Gao et al. (2022).
When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. The general principle behind reward hacking and overoptimization.
The tendency of raters and reward models to prefer longer responses regardless of quality.
A model agreeing with or flattering the user's stated views instead of being accurate, often learned from preference data.
A reward model that scores only the final response.
A reward model that scores each intermediate step of a reasoning chain (Lightman et al. 2023).
Reinforcement learning from AI feedback: preference labels produced by a model guided by written principles instead of by people.
Reinforcement learning from human feedback: training a policy to maximize a learned reward model's score with a KL penalty to a reference model.
In RL for language models, the model's next-token distribution \(\pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)\).
A frozen copy of the starting model used to measure and penalize how far the trained policy drifts.
A term \(\beta\,\mathrm{KL}(\pi_\theta \| \pi_{\text{ref}})\) that keeps the trained policy close to the reference; \(\beta\) sets its strength.
A response sampled from the current policy during RL training, then scored.
An estimator of the gradient of expected reward using samples from the policy, weighting each action's log-probability gradient by its return or advantage.
The basic Monte Carlo policy gradient algorithm (Williams 1992).
How much better an action turned out than expected from that state: \(A_t = R_t - V(s_t)\).
A quantity subtracted from the return in a policy gradient to reduce variance without adding bias, usually the value estimate.
A network that predicts expected future reward from each state, used to compute advantages in PPO.
Generalized advantage estimation: an exponentially weighted sum of one-step temporal-difference errors, with \(\lambda\) trading bias for variance.
Proximal Policy Optimization (Schulman et al. 2017): a policy gradient method that clips the probability ratio so each batch can only move the policy a limited amount.
\(\pi_\theta(a\mid s)/\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(a\mid s)\), how much an update changed an action's probability. PPO clips it to \([1-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon]\).
A policy earning reward through behavior the designer did not intend, such as padding answers for a length-biased reward model.
Capability regressions caused by alignment training, first documented on public NLP benchmarks in InstructGPT.
OpenAI's 2022 SFT, reward model, PPO recipe (Ouyang et al. 2022), the template for most later RLHF pipelines.
Direct Preference Optimization (Rafailov et al. 2023): optimizes the KL-regularised RLHF objective with a classification loss on preference pairs, without a reward model or RL loop.
In DPO, \(\beta \log \pi_\theta(y\mid x)/\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)\), the reward the policy implicitly defines.
A DPO failure where both chosen and rejected log-likelihoods fall during training and probability moves to responses neither label mentioned.
Identity Preference Optimization (Azar et al. 2023): a squared loss toward a finite target margin, avoiding DPO's overfitting to deterministic preferences.
Kahneman–Tversky Optimization (Ethayarajh et al. 2024): preference optimization from unpaired desirable and undesirable examples.
Odds Ratio Preference Optimization (Hong et al. 2024): single-stage SFT plus an odds-ratio preference penalty, with no reference model.
Simple Preference Optimization (Meng et al. 2024): reference-free, length-normalized implicit reward with a target margin.
Repeated rounds of sampling from the current policy, labeling pairs with a reward model or judge, and training with the DPO loss.
Training data generated by a different model than the one being trained.
